title: Shear-deformed fossils are often mistaken for distinct species

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Shear-deformed fossils are often mistaken for distinct species

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Fossils in folded and inclined strata are often symmetrically deformed, usually by simple shear, so that they have been described as distinct species and occasionally even as new genera.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the contained fossils are apt to be so curiously and yet so symmetrically deformed (usually by a simple shear) that they may easily be interpreted as so many distinct and separate “species.”

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVII, “On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms”; topic “Deformed fossils and spurious species”. Scope: fossils in tectonically deformed strata

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch17-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.64

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Shear and taxonomic consequences are measurable and historical names can be checked. Public data enable case studies, but systematic tectonic context and the denominator needed to judge frequency require substantial compilation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Identify fossil specimens from deformed strata, estimate strain fields from sedimentary markers, reverse the deformation, and audit whether named taxa collapse morphometrically into existing species or genera.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
“Often” has no stated frequency threshold.

Strain markers and taxonomic histories are not jointly encoded.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim is a countable historical pattern: sheared fossils have often been named as separate species. Occurrence databases list candidate taxa and localities, while the strain measurements and later synonymies live in local geological papers. A team can assemble a partial test for well-studied slates and cannot yet survey deformed strata in general.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For fossils from folded strata, compare shape differences with an independent tectonic strain estimate and ask whether names later treated as separate species collapse once that shear is removed. Support would be repeated cases where the residual biological difference is within species-level variation; persistent differences after retrodeformation would count against mistaking shear for taxonomy.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Strain markers and the taxonomic histories of supposed species are scattered by locality, not stored with the occurrence data.

Biological variation and compaction can mimic tectonic shear.
